messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
I'm new to rocketry. Landing speed below 5.5 m/s, please. I want to beat 400 m. We launch off a 2 m rail. Explain what you pick, please.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee at least 400 m, and "beat 400 m" means a minimum, not a target to trim. Landing below 5.5 m/s (maximum), tighter than the usual 6 m/s. The rail is 2 m (fixed). Wind, angle and site are not stated, so 2 m/s, vertical, sea level. The flyer is new, so a single-stage sport rocket with one chute. No motor is specified.
2. Feasibility: no-drag speed for 400 m is sqrt(2*9.81*400) = 89 m/s. A C6 in a small tube often finishes around 300 to 400 m, so it is marginal. A D has about twice the impulse and is the usual first motor that clears 400 m with room. A 2 m rail is long, so even a modest average thrust still leaves the rod fast. I will look up a D and an E.

2. Feasibility: the Estes D12 is 16.8 N*s at 10.4 N average, a 24 mm case, 0.07 m long, 0.0426 kg, with 0, 3, 5 and 7 s delays. The E12 is 27.1 N*s in the same 24 mm diameter and would fly higher than a first rocket needs. The D12 is the one I would hand a new flyer: enough impulse to beat 400 m, and the 5 s delay matches a flight of this size. The E stays on the shelf.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.12 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 10.4 / (0.12 * 9.81) = 8.83. Pad weight 0.12 * 9.81 = 1.18 N, rail acceleration (10.4 - 1.18) / 0.12 = 76.8 m/s^2, and the 2 m rail gives sqrt(2 * 76.8 * 2) = 17.5 m/s on the average thrust. The D12 spike should clear 15 m/s. Propellant is 0.021 kg, descent mass 0.12 - 0.021 = 0.099 kg. For 4.5 m/s, under the 5.5 m/s cap, area = 2 * 0.099 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.5^2) = 0.0979 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.0979 / 3.1416) = 0.35 m. I will use 0.45 m so a heavier build still lands slowly.
4. Draft: 0.10 m ogive polystyrene nose on a 0.40 m cardboard tube, outer diameter 0.041 m, wall 0.8 mm. Mount 0.027 m outside, 0.08 m long, Estes D12 with a 5 s delay. Three balsa fins, root 0.070 m, tip 0.030 m, span 0.050 m, sweep 0.035 m, 3 mm thick. One 0.45 m polyethylene chute on ejection. Rail 2 m.

4. Check: the D12 did not clear 400 m, and it is not stable. The simulator gives 344.2 m, so 400 - 344.2 = 55.8 m short. Margin is 0.64 cal at rail exit and through the burn, under 1.0 cal. Landing is 3.1 m/s, under 5.5 m/s. Rail exit is 28.8 m/s on the 2 m rail, thrust-to-weight 11.0. Mass is 0.0967 kg, lighter than my 0.12 kg guess, so the miss is drag from the 41 mm tube, not weight. The chute opens at 6.7 s, just before the 6.94 s apogee.
5. Fix: two misses, 344.2 m and 0.64 cal. I am keeping the D12, because the motor is not the weak part, and slimming the tube. New tube outer diameter 0.033 m, length 0.36 m, wall 0.6 mm. Mount drops to 0.026 m outside so it still fits. Fins grow so the smaller tube stays stable: root 0.075 m, tip 0.030 m, span 0.055 m, sweep 0.040 m. Nose diameter follows the tube, 0.033 m. Chute and the 5 s delay stay.

4. Check: closer, still short on both. The simulator gives 392.9 m, and 400 - 392.9 = 7.1 m under the 400 m minimum. Margin is 0.92 cal, just under 1.0 cal. Landing 2.7 m/s, rail exit 31.2 m/s and thrust-to-weight 13.2 pass. Mass is 0.0801 kg. The 33 mm tube picked up 344.2 m to 392.9 m, so the D12 is simply a little light for a stable fin set on this rocket.
5. Fix: the failing numbers are 392.9 m and 0.92 cal. I am stepping to the Estes E12, 27.1 N*s, same 24 mm case, 6 s delay, and giving the fins a bit more span so the heavier motor does not push the margin back down. Mount length becomes 0.11 m to fit the 0.095 m case. Tube length 0.42 m. Fins: root 0.080 m, tip 0.032 m, span 0.060 m, sweep 0.042 m. Nose, chute and 0.033 m diameter stay.

4. Check: the E12 clears the altitude. The simulator gives 524.4 m, and 524.4 - 400 = 124 m over the 400 m minimum. Landing is 2.9 m/s, rail exit 30.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight 11.3. The chute opens at 8.4 s, just after the 8.32 s apogee. Margin is 0.98 cal at rail exit and through the burn, still a hair under 1.0 cal. Mass is 0.101 kg.
5. Fix: the failing value is 0.98 cal. Altitude has 124 m of spare, so a little nose mass is the small move. I am adding 0.005 kg of clay at the top of the tube and leaving the fins, the tube and the E12 alone. That should push the CG forward just enough without giving the altitude back.

4. Check: the clay did it. The simulator gives 1.38 cal at rail exit and through the burn, over the 1 cal floor. Apogee is 526.4 m, and 526.4 - 400 = 126 m over the minimum. Landing is 3.0 m/s, under 5.5 m/s. Rail exit is 29.1 m/s on the 2 m rail, thrust-to-weight 10.7. The chute opens at 8.4 s, just before the 8.48 s apogee, at 0.5 m/s. Mass is 0.106 kg.
5. Fix: no further change. Altitude, landing speed and the stability gates all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 526.4 m is well clear of 400 m, so a heavier cardboard tube or a coat of paint should still beat it. The margin is 1.38 cal with 0.005 kg of clay; leaving that clay out was 0.98 cal in the previous run, so the build needs that weight in the nose. Landing at 3.0 m/s depends on the 0.45 m chute actually opening. A 2 m/s wind was assumed.
messages.content:
Estes E12-6 in a 33 mm cardboard rocket, with 5 g of nose clay and a 0.45 m chute. A D12 on a wider tube did not reach 400 m, so this is the E.
On the 2 m rail it reaches 526.4 m, holds 1.38 cal, and lands at 3.0 m/s, under the 5.5 m/s cap.
The clay is what moved the margin over 1 cal. Leave it out and the rocket sits just under that floor.
